title: Money and Banking
description: Class 12 Economics: functions and supply of money, commercial banks and credit creation with the money multiplier, and the RBI's functions and monetary policy instruments (repo, CRR, SLR, OMO).

topics.title: Money: Functions and Supply
topics.concept:
Money is anything generally accepted as a medium of exchange and in the settlement of debts. It evolved through stages — from barter to commodity money, metallic money, paper money, and today bank money and digital money — each stage making exchange easier.

Money performs four functions: it is a medium of exchange (the primary function — it removes the barter problem of a double coincidence of wants), a measure of value (prices express value in money), a store of value (it can be saved), and a standard of deferred payments (it lets borrowing and lending happen). People hold money for two main reasons (the demand for money): the transactions motive (to make everyday payments) and the precautionary and speculative motives (for emergencies and to take advantage of future opportunities).

The supply of money is the total stock of money held by the public at a point of time (it is a stock, and it excludes money held by the government and banks themselves). The Reserve Bank measures it in several monetary aggregates, the most-quoted being:

  • M1 = currency (notes and coins) with the public + demand deposits in banks + other deposits with the RBI. M1 is the most liquid measure, also called narrow money.
  • Wider measures M2, M3 and M4 add less-liquid deposits (like savings and time deposits); M3 (M1 + time deposits) is called broad money and is the most commonly used aggregate.

So money is what oils the whole economy — and how much of it there is (the money supply) is a key macroeconomic variable that the central bank controls.

examples.problem: Example 1: State the four functions of money.
examples.solution:
Recall the list.

  • Medium of exchange (primary), measure of value.
  • Store of value, standard of deferred payments.
examples.answer: Medium of exchange, measure of value, store of value, and standard of deferred payments.

examples.solution:
The most liquid components.

  • Currency with the public + demand deposits + other deposits with the RBI.
examples.answer: Currency with the public, demand deposits with banks, and other deposits with the RBI.

examples.problem: Example 3: Is the supply of money a stock or a flow?
examples.solution:
It is measured at a point of time.

  • It is the total money held by the public at a point of time — a stock.
examples.answer: A stock (the total money held by the public at a point of time).

recap:
• Money: generally accepted medium of exchange; evolved barter → commodity → metallic → paper → bank/digital.
  • Functions: medium of exchange (primary), measure of value, store of value, deferred payments. Demand: transactions, precautionary, speculative.
  • Money supply (a stock, excludes govt/banks): M1 = currency + demand deposits + other deposits with RBI (narrow); M3 = broad money.

quiz.q: The primary function of money is as a:
quiz.explanation: The medium of exchange is the primary function of money.

quiz.q: M1 (narrow money) includes currency with the public plus:
options: Demand deposits and other deposits with RBI
quiz.explanation: M1 = currency + demand deposits + other deposits with the RBI.

topics.title: Commercial Banks and Credit Creation
topics.concept:
A commercial bank accepts deposits from the public and lends money to earn profit. Its two primary functions are accepting deposits (current, savings and fixed deposits) and advancing loans (loans, cash credit, overdrafts). The gap between interest charged on loans and paid on deposits is the bank's profit.

The most important macroeconomic role of banks is credit creation (money creation). Banks know that not all depositors withdraw at once, so they keep only a small fraction of deposits as a cash reserve and lend out the rest. The borrowed money is spent and returns to the banking system as a fresh deposit, of which a fraction is again kept and the rest re-lent — and so on. In this way the banking system as a whole creates total deposits that are a multiple of the original cash.

The size of this multiple is the money (credit) multiplier, which depends on the reserve ratio (the fraction of deposits kept as reserves):

Money Multiplier = 1 ÷ LRR  (LRR = legal reserve ratio)

So if banks must keep 20% (0.2) as reserves, the multiplier is 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5: an initial deposit of ₹1,000 can support total deposits of ₹1,000 × 5 = ₹5,000. The smaller the reserve ratio, the larger the credit a given cash base can create. This is why the central bank controls the reserve ratio to control the money supply — the subject of monetary policy.

examples.problem: Example 1: What are the two primary functions of a commercial bank?
examples.solution:
Deposits in, loans out.

  • Accepting deposits and advancing loans.
examples.answer: Accepting deposits from the public and advancing loans.

examples.problem: Example 2: If the legal reserve ratio is 25%, find the money multiplier and the total deposits an initial deposit of ₹2,000 can create.
Example 3: What happens to credit creation if the reserve ratio is reduced?
examples.solution:
A smaller reserve means more lending.

  • The multiplier (1 ÷ LRR) rises.
  • So banks can create more credit.
examples.answer: Credit creation increases, because a lower reserve ratio raises the money multiplier (1 ÷ LRR).

recap:
• Commercial bank: accepts deposits, advances loans; profit = interest gap.
  • Credit creation: keep a fraction as reserves, re-lend the rest → total deposits = a multiple of the cash.
  • Money multiplier = 1 ÷ LRR (e.g. LRR 20% → multiplier 5). Lower reserve ratio → more credit.

quiz.q: If the legal reserve ratio is 10%, the money multiplier is:
Banks can create credit because they keep only a ____ of deposits as reserves.
quiz.explanation: Keeping a small fraction as reserves lets banks lend the rest and create credit.

topics.title: The Reserve Bank of India and Monetary Policy
topics.concept:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is the central bank — the apex institution that controls the country's money and banking system in the public interest (not for profit). Its main functions are: currency authority (sole right to issue notes), banker to the government, bankers' bank (banks keep reserves with it), lender of last resort, custodian of foreign exchange reserves, and — most important — controller of credit.

The RBI controls the money supply and credit in the economy through its monetary policy. The instruments are of two kinds. The quantitative measures (which affect the total volume of credit) are:

  • Repo rate — the rate at which the RBI lends to commercial banks. Raising it makes borrowing costlier, reducing credit.
  • Reverse repo rate — the rate at which the RBI borrows from banks (absorbing their funds).
  • Bank rate — the rate at which the RBI lends to banks for the long term.
  • Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) — the fraction of deposits banks must keep as cash with the RBI. Raising the CRR leaves banks less to lend, reducing credit.
  • Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) — the fraction of deposits banks must keep in safe assets (cash, gold, government securities).
  • Open Market Operations (OMO) — the RBI buying or selling government securities to inject or absorb money.

The qualitative measures (which affect the direction/use of credit) include margin requirements, moral suasion and selective credit controls. To fight inflation, the RBI tightens (raises repo rate, CRR, SLR; sells securities) to reduce the money supply; to fight a slowdown, it eases (lowers them; buys securities) to increase the money supply. Monetary policy is therefore one of the government's two great tools (with fiscal policy) for managing the whole economy.

examples.solution:
It is the RBI's lending rate to banks.

  • The rate at which the RBI lends to commercial banks.
  • Raising it makes credit costlier and reduces the money supply.
examples.answer: The repo rate is the rate at which the RBI lends to commercial banks; raising it reduces credit and the money supply.

examples.problem: Example 2: Name three quantitative instruments of monetary policy.
examples.solution:
They affect the total volume of credit.

  • Repo rate, CRR and SLR (also reverse repo, bank rate, OMO).
examples.answer: Repo rate, Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) — also bank rate and open market operations.

examples.problem: Example 3: To control inflation, should the RBI raise or lower the CRR? Why?
examples.solution:
Inflation needs less money in circulation.

  • Raise the CRR.
  • This leaves banks less to lend, reducing credit and the money supply, cooling inflation.
examples.answer: Raise the CRR — it leaves banks less to lend, reducing the money supply and helping to cool inflation.

recap:
• RBI (central bank): currency authority, banker to govt, bankers' bank, lender of last resort, forex custodian, controller of credit.
  • Quantitative tools: repo/reverse-repo/bank rate, CRR, SLR, OMO; qualitative: margin requirements, moral suasion, selective controls.
  • Fight inflation → tighten (raise rates/CRR/SLR, sell securities); fight slowdown → ease.

quiz.q: The rate at which the RBI lends to commercial banks is the:
quiz.explanation: The repo rate is the RBI's lending rate to banks.

quiz.q: To control inflation, the RBI would:
options: Raise the repo rate and CRR
quiz.explanation: Raising the repo rate and CRR reduces credit and the money supply, cooling inflation.

questions.q: Money is anything generally accepted as a:
questions.explanation: Money is a generally accepted medium of exchange.

questions.q: The primary function of money is as a:
questions.explanation: The medium of exchange is the primary function.

questions.q: Holding money for everyday payments is the ____ motive.
questions.explanation: Money for daily payments is the transactions motive.

questions.q: The supply of money is a:
questions.explanation: Money supply is a stock (held at a point of time).

questions.q: M1 (narrow money) includes currency with the public plus:
options: Demand deposits and other deposits with RBI
questions.explanation: M1 = currency + demand deposits + other deposits with RBI.

questions.q: Broad money is denoted by:
questions.explanation: M3 (M1 + time deposits) is broad money.

questions.q: The two primary functions of a commercial bank are accepting deposits and:
questions.explanation: Banks accept deposits and advance loans.

questions.q: The money multiplier equals:
questions.explanation: Money multiplier = 1 ÷ legal reserve ratio.

questions.q: If LRR = 20%, the money multiplier is:
A lower reserve ratio means credit creation:
questions.explanation: A lower reserve ratio raises the multiplier, increasing credit.

questions.q: The central bank of India is the:
questions.explanation: The Reserve Bank of India is the central bank.

questions.q: The sole right to issue currency notes is the RBI's role as:
questions.explanation: Issuing currency is the currency-authority function.

questions.q: The rate at which the RBI lends to banks is the:
questions.explanation: The repo rate is the RBI's lending rate to banks.

questions.q: The fraction of deposits banks must keep as cash with the RBI is the:
questions.explanation: CRR is the cash reserve ratio kept with the RBI.

questions.q: To control inflation, the RBI would:
options: Raise the repo rate and CRR
questions.explanation: Tightening (higher repo/CRR) reduces money supply to cool inflation.

questions.q: With a legal reserve ratio of 25% and an initial deposit of ₹4,000, the maximum total deposits the banking system can create is:
questions.explanation: Multiplier = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4; total deposits = 4,000 × 4 = ₹16,000.

questions.q: To fight a recession (slowdown), the RBI should:
options: Lower the repo rate and CRR and buy securities
questions.explanation: Easing (lower rates/CRR, buying securities) raises the money supply to boost spending in a slowdown.

questions.q: Open market operations control the money supply when the RBI:
options: Buys securities (injects money) or sells them (absorbs money)
questions.explanation: Buying government securities releases money into the system; selling them takes money out.

questions.q: Raising the CRR reduces credit because it forces banks to:
options: Keep more cash with the RBI, leaving less to lend
questions.explanation: A higher CRR locks up more of each deposit, shrinking the lendable funds and credit creation.

questions.q: Banks can create credit only because, in normal times, depositors:
options: Do not all withdraw their money at the same time
questions.explanation: Since withdrawals are spread out, banks safely lend most of the deposits, multiplying credit.

questions.q: When the RBI raises the repo rate, commercial banks typically respond by:
options: Raising their own lending rates, so loans become costlier
questions.explanation: Costlier borrowing from the RBI is passed on, so bank loan rates rise and credit demand falls.

questions.q: The RBI acting as 'lender of last resort' means it:
options: Lends to banks in a crisis when they can get funds nowhere else
questions.explanation: In a panic the RBI supports stressed banks, preventing the system from collapsing.

questions.q: Margin requirements and moral suasion are examples of ____ measures of monetary policy.
questions.explanation: These affect the direction/use of credit rather than its total volume — qualitative measures.

questions.q: Money supply excludes cash held by the government and banks because money supply measures money held by the:
questions.explanation: Only money in the hands of the public counts; inter-bank and government cash is excluded.

questions.q: Both monetary policy (RBI) and fiscal policy (government budget) are used to manage the economy. Monetary policy works mainly by changing the:
questions.explanation: The RBI steers the economy chiefly through the quantity of money and the cost of credit (interest rates).
